Cyclist Magazine Podcast: The hardest Tour de France, with Gareth Cartman

This week on the Cyclist Magazine Podcast, James is joined by cycling historian and author, Gareth Cartman. Gareth’s life long love of cycling began watching Marco Pantani in the Tour de France on Channel 4 (remember when the Tour was on the tele?), and was cemented while living in Paris, witnessing, as he says, Lance Armstrong ‘not win the Tour seven times’.

Gareth’s latest book, We Rode All Night, tells the story of the longest, most gruelling Tour in history, the 1926 edition, in which just 41 riders finished, with several almost not making it back at all after the infamous Stage 10 – 326km and nearly 8,000m elevation, ridden through the night amid unprecedented storms.

In this chat Gareth brings to life cycling’s earliest days, from the iron-fisted rule of Tour founder Henri Desgrange, to the wacky-races cheating, near-death experiences, harrowing rider backstories, political and social unrest, Communist newspaper journalists, terrible roads, the mud, the blood, the countless soggy woollen jerseys and tear streaked faces… they don’t make ’em like they used to, so get the kettle on and pin back your lugholes.

Gareth’s previous books include We Rode All Day, retelling the story of the 1919 Tour de France through the voices of the riders; Walko, recounting Roger Walkowiak’s remarkable and unexpected victory in the 1956 Tour de France; and Koblet + Kubler, which explores the intertwined lives and careers of Switzerland’s two great cycling champions.

Check out We Rode All Night (Pitch Publishing) at pitchpublishing.co.uk

Chat begins at 11:40.
